sq.ANSWER:
A circular queue is a linear data structure that follows the FIFO (First In, First Out) principle. Unlike a regular (linear) queue, when the rear reaches the end of the array, it wraps around to the beginning if there is free space—hence called circular.

Dequeue Operation

The dequeue operation refers to removing an element from the front of the circular queue.

  • It retrieves and removes the element at the position indicated by front.
  • After deletion, it updates the front pointer to point to the next element.

 

Handling the front Pointer in Circular Queue:

  • The front pointer is crucial because it always points to the first element of the queue (i.e., the one to be removed next).

 

Case 1: Queue is Empty (Underflow Condition)

Before performing a dequeue, we check:

if (front == -1)

If front is -1, it means the queue is empty, and a dequeue operation cannot be performed.

 

Case 2: Queue Has Only One Element

If the queue has just one element:

if (front == rear)

Then, after removing the element, we reset both front and rear to -1 to indicate that the queue is now empty.

 

Case 3: Normal Dequeue Operation

In a regular case where the queue has more than one element:

front = (front + 1) % size;

This line ensures that the front moves to the next valid index in a circular manner.

  • If front is at the last index (size - 1), the modulo operation wraps it back to 0.
  • This prevents overflow and maintains the circular nature of the queue.

 

Example

Suppose size = 5, and elements are:

Index:  0   1   2   3   4

Queue: [A, B, C, D, E]

front = 0, rear = 4

  • Dequeue Operation:
    • Removes A (element at index 0)
    • New front = (0 + 1) % 5 = 1
    • Queue becomes: [_, B, C, D, E]
    • Now front points to B

If we keep dequeuing and front reaches index 4:

  • After one more dequeue: front = (4 + 1) % 5 = 0 → wrapped to start

sq.ANSWER:
A DEQUE (Double-Ended Queue) is a linear data structure that allows insertion and deletion of elements from both the front and rear ends.

  • The term "deque" is pronounced as "deck".
  • It is more flexible than a standard queue because it does not restrict operations to one end for insertion and another for deletion.

How DEQUE Works:

A DEQUE can be visualized as a container where:

  • You can insert elements at the front or the rear.
  • You can remove elements from the front or the rear.

This bidirectional capability makes it suitable for problems where data needs to be processed from both ends.

Types of DEQUEs:

There are two common types of DEQUEs:

  1. Input-Restricted DEQUE:
    • Insertion is allowed only at the rear.
    • Deletion can be done from both ends.

  1. Output-Restricted DEQUE:
    • Deletion is allowed only from the front.
    • Insertion can be done at both ends.

These variations help in modeling specific scenarios where partial restrictions are needed.

 

Key Differences Between DEQUE and Standard Queue:

Standard Queue

DEQUE (Double-Ended Queue)

Insertion

Only at the rear

At both front and rear

Deletion

Only from the front

From both front and rear

Less flexible

More flexible

Use Cases

Palindrome checking, browser history

Types

Input-restricted and Output-restricted
sq.QUESTION_DESC: What is a DEQUE? How is it different from a standard queue?

lq.ANSWER:
In a print queue system, print jobs are added as users send their files to be printed. Normally, these jobs are processed in the order they arrive (FIFO — First In First Out). However, in real-time systems, priority jobs (e.g., admin printouts, urgent reports) may need to jump the queue and be printed before the regular ones.

Why Use a DEQUE (Double-Ended Queue)?

A DEQUE is the ideal data structure in this scenario because:

Requirement

How DEQUE Handles It

Regular jobs added at the rear

insertRear() operation

Priority jobs added at the front

insertFront() operation

Jobs printed (deleted) from the front

deleteFront() operation

Optional job removal from the rear

deleteRear() (used for cancellation, if needed)

In short, a DEQUE provides the flexibility to manage both regular and priority jobs efficiently.

Pseudocode for DEQUE Operations in Print Queue

Structure of a Node (for DEQUE implemented using Linked List)

struct Node {

    string jobName;

    Node* next;

    Node* prev;

};

Two pointers to maintain:

  • front → Points to the front job in the queue
  • rear → Points to the last job in the queue

Insert a Job at the Rear (Normal Job):

A new node is created for the job.

If the queue is empty, the new node becomes both front and rear.

Otherwise, it's linked to the current rear, and rear is updated.

 

Function insertRear(string jobName):

    newNode = createNode(jobName)

    if front == NULL:   // Queue is empty

        front = rear = newNode

    else:

        rear.next = newNode

        newNode.prev = rear

        rear = newNode

    print "Job added at rear:", jobname

 

Insert a Job at the Front (Priority Job):

A new node is created and added before the current front.

The front pointer is updated to point to the new job.

This ensures the priority job is printed next.

 

Function insertFront(string jobName):

    newNode = createNode(jobName)

    if front == NULL:   // Queue is empty

        front = rear = newNode

    else:

        newNode.next = front

        front.prev = newNode

        front = newNode

    print "Priority job added at front:", jobname

 

Dequeue (Print a Job from Front)

Function deleteFront():

    if front == NULL:

        print "Queue is empty. No job to print."

    else:

        temp = front

        front = front.next

        if front != NULL:

            front.prev = NULL

        else:

            rear = NULL   // Queue is now empty

        print "Printing job:", temp.jobName

        delete temp
